EntertainmentTab.title: Your mission, Tom Cruise, is to improve at interviews. And please keep sending the cakes
EntertainmentTab.text:
By now, we’ve grown used to watching Tom Cruise excel at everything he does. Running in films? The best. Risking his life in action scenes so preposterously dangerous that audiences need to have their sphincters manually unclenched with a crowbar? Absolutely, none better. Singlehandedly ensuring that theatrical exhibition didn’t go extinct after Covid? The man deserves all the praise in the world for that.

But nobody is perfect. Live long enough and a few flaws will worm their way to the surface. This is as true for Tom Cruise as it is for anyone else. And while I realise that this might do me out of a cake this Christmas, the following really needs to be said: Tom Cruise isn’t very good at interviews.

As you will be aware, Cruise’s new film Digger comes out soon. The film is a risk. It is his first original, non-sequel, non-action film in which he co-stars since 2007’s Lions for Lambs. It is also, if the trailers are any indication, palpably batshit. This means that Cruise has to reintroduce himself to the world as an actor, rather than the guy who just flings himself off a variety of increasingly berserk surfaces. And this means promotion. Until this week, that promotion has involved either World Cup-themed promos filmed in character or interviews where the subject matter was almost exclusively limited to lens choice.

However, yesterday Cruise subjected himself to a rare longform interview opposite GQ’s Zach Baron. On paper, it couldn’t have been easier. Baron was a perfectly chosen interviewer for the job, understanding exactly when to flatter and when to needle. However, Tom Cruise’s defences are foot-thick and watertight, and the majority of Baron’s questions simply bounced off him.

This resulted in a fairly unsatisfactory 30-minute stalemate in which Tom Cruise talked and talked and said nothing at all. No matter how hard Baron probed, he was met with a fat wedge of waffle. The clickbait industrial complex has done its best to pick the bones of the interview for a news peg, but the best it seems to have come up with is a variation of “Tom Cruise admits that he can be intense on set”. Which, well, duh.

Aside from that, we simply got a rehash of all the old talking points from every junket he’s done for a decade. He’d rather talk about cinematography than himself. He is constantly trying to learn new skills. He writes down his dreams and how to accomplish them. None of this is new information. It’s all highly frustrating. But it does make sense. As brilliant as he is on screen, behind the scenes Cruise is a carefully managed enigma. This may well be because, the last time he allowed his own self to parade before the press, it ended with couch-jumping and excruciatingly testy interviews about Scientology. It seems unthinkable now, but that press run went so badly that Sumner Redstone ended up effectively firing Cruise from Paramount over it.

It took Cruise years to build himself back up from that, and the results have been spectacular. The Mission: Impossible films have been some of the greatest of his career. Top Gun: Maverick saved Hollywood. He is now in a position of enormous power and authority. So going back out in front of an interviewer is bound to be a risk for him. But one thing is certain. The Digger promotional cycle cannot just be variations of the GQ interview, because too many opaque soundbites will simply end up boring potential audiences rigid. There will be more interviews – he’s thought to be hitting the podcast circuit soon – so he needs to adapt his strategy.

The good news is that one thing Cruise did say in his GQ interview is that, when he sets a goal, he writes down all the steps necessary to accomplish it. This is exactly what he should do here. If his dream is doing press that will make people want to watch Digger, then he knows he will need to work up some new anecdotes – long enough to filibuster, but twisty enough to entertain – while developing a persona that appears to welcome scrutiny while wriggling out from underneath it.

It can be done. Robert Downey Jr is an actor with many areas of his past he would rather not touch in print, and he has built up an incredibly charming suit of armour that allows him to breezily bat questions away when they get too personal. This is exactly what Tom Cruise should be learning to do. Or perhaps not; after all, he has made hundreds of millions of dollars by revealing scarcely anything about himself for a decade. Maybe that’s an option, too.

But, hey, this is Tom Cruise. When he sets his mind on something, he achieves it. With that in mind, expect a dramatic upward turn in the quality of his interviews from this moment onwards. Thanks for reading. Please still send cakes.

GeneralTab.title: Charles said Diana would be forgotten 'soon enough', Earl Spencer claims in book
GeneralTab.text:
Buckingham Palace has responded after a claim by Earl Spencer, the brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, that King Charles said "we'll forget her soon enough" days after her death.

Earl Spencer alleged the then-Prince of Wales subjected him to a "stream of anger" after he insisted Diana would not have wanted Princes William and Harry, then aged 15 and 12, to walk in her funeral procession.

The claim was made in an extract from his upcoming memoir, published by the Daily Mail.

A Palace spokesperson said: "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss."

Swan Song: Diana, My Sister is due to be published next week and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family. BBC News has not seen the book in full.

In the first extract, external from it to be made public, Earl Spencer claims to have been informed by a senior Palace aide that the young princes would walk alongside Princess Diana's coffin, which he objected to.

He claims to have received a phone call from Charles shortly after.

Earl Spencer wrote in the book: "He [Charles] unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death. 'Rest assured,' he hissed, 'we'll forget her soon enough'."

Earl Spencer's book about his sister seems set to open a very difficult time in the recent history of the Royal Family.

The death of Diana, a hugely popular figure, in a car crash in 1997, had created a volatile atmosphere, in which the royals were accused of failing to show feeling and empathy, and had seemed out of touch with the public mood.

Earl Spencer's emotional and defiant speech at her funeral added to that cloud of grievance hanging over Diana's untimely death.

Prince Harry has previously said that walking behind his mother's coffin aged 12 was something no child "should be asked to do".

In 2017, he told the BBC he didn't "have an opinion whether that was right or wrong", but "looking back on it", he was glad to have been part of the day.

Earlier on Wednesday, it emerged that copies of Earl Spencer's unreleased book had been stolen from a truck in the Netherlands.

BBC News understands four copies of the Dutch language edition were taken from a truck while it was en route from the Dutch publisher's printers to their warehouse.

GeneralTab.title: New hope for breast cancer patients as life-extending drug now on NHS in England
GeneralTab.text:
Patients in England with a specific type of incurable breast cancer can now access a life-extending drug on the NHS, two years after it was deemed too expensive by a health body.

Enhertu can give patients almost seven extra months to live on average - with some living up to three years longer.

Women in Scotland have had access to the drug on the NHS since 2023, and it is available in 26 other European countries.

Charities and patients have campaigned for it to be more widely available since 2024, when the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) said Enhertu was not good value for money.

From Thursday, doctors in England are now able to prescribe it, with Wales expected to follow shortly but the guidance doesn't automatically apply to Northern Ireland.

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said: "Enhertu can be life-changing, and this recommendation means NHS patients will finally be able to benefit from it.

"It is a tribute to the campaigners and charities who never stopped pressing for this."

This decision will affect about 1,000 women a year with a specific type of breast cancer, HER2-low.

Charity Breast Cancer Now said that while campaigners' "persistence paid off", thousands of people have missed out on access to Enhertu and many have died.

The charity's chief executive, Claire Rowney, said: "Today we can finally say we did it." However, she adds that "we can't celebrate this momentous decision without remembering the devastating cost of this delay".

Kate Wills, 51, understands this mix of emotions. She has HER2-low metastatic breast cancer, which has spread to her bones and lungs. But nothing about her suggests that she is terminally ill.

She has a high-powered job and is a wife and mum. Her social media feed shows a full and happy life - only the occasional medical appointment hints all is not well.

Kate says it has been "incredibly painful" to know that Enhertu could keep her alive for longer but she couldn't get it.

When she hears it will be available on the NHS, she immediately starts crying. "I really can't believe it. I'm so relieved, I'm overjoyed," she says.

"It's so hard keeping hope when you have stage four cancer. This gives me enormous hope."

Her son and daughter are in their teens and early 20s. Kate has been aiming to stay alive long enough for her youngest to finish school.

She smiles through her tears as she says: "Now I've just dared to dream that I might be around to see them fall in love, to get married."

For her, this is bittersweet. Her first thought is for "those women, my friends, who didn't get this in time".

The BBC understands that the drug companies Daiichi Sankyo and AstraZeneca have not substantially lowered their prices since the drug was first rejected.

The reason NICE has reversed its decision is largely because of a trade deal with the USA, where the UK government agreed to spend 25% more on medicines.

As part of this, NICE has increased how much the NHS will pay for every extra year of good quality life a medication can give.

This is known as a QALY (Quality-Adjusted Life Year) - and the upper threshold per QALY has gone from £30,000 to £35,000.

At the end of August, NICE also introduced a different, more nuanced, way of measuring a patient's quality of life.

These two changes were enough to tip the balance.

It is thought that patient campaigns for Enhertu - and other drugs - have helped too.

Daiichi Sankyo and AstraZeneca welcome NICE's decision, but the latter is calling for "strong collaboration" across the healthcare system to ensure "faster, more equitable patient access in the future".

Breast Cancer Now's Claire Rowney says: "We are calling on the government, NICE, NHS England and the pharmaceutical industry to work together to fix this broken system, so that people with incurable metastatic breast cancer are not forced to spend precious months and years campaigning for treatments that could give them more time."

Helen Knight, director of medicines evaluation at NICE, says she is pleased a "commercial solution" means the treatment can be made available on the NHS in England but adds she knows the decision "comes too late for many families".

"Our role is important in ensuring NHS spending on new medicines reflects the benefits they deliver while protecting valuable health resources for other essential patient services," she says.

For Kate, the thought of dying before she had to, "when there was a drug that I just could almost reach but couldn't get", was "so incredibly painful".

"To know that I can get it now is absolutely everything."

GeneralTab.title: Robert Kraft says Ed Sheeran asked him to donate $2m to aid after Macklemore backlash
GeneralTab.text:
The US stadium owner who had pro-Palestinian rapper Macklemore removed as Ed Sheeran's opening act at his venue says Sheeran has asked him to donate $2m to "aid in the region".

New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft announced the requested pledge in his second statement this week on the controversy, without specifying where exactly the funds would go.

Kraft confirmed on Monday he had Macklemore dropped as opening act from Sheeran's forthcoming Loop Tour at the Gillette Stadium near Boston, accusing the rapper of hate speech.

Facing a backlash, Sheeran has said the decision to drop Macklemore was made by promoters and that he would not be drawn into a public debate over Gaza.

On Wednesday, Macklemore said he would donate $1m to Palestinian organisations, challenging Kraft to match the sum.

In a statement later that day, Kraft, 85, said: "Earlier today, before Macklemore challenged me to match his donation, Ed called me and asked me to commit $2 million to match his donation to aid in the region to fight this humanitarian crisis.

"Ed now plans to reach out to other venue owners and our goal is to continue to work together to build bridges."

In the statement, which was issued by Gillette Stadium on Kraft's behalf, he said he would like those speaking in support of the Palestinian people to know that he has long "supported efforts that create opportunity for Palestinians".

He also said that he has worked to bring "young Palestinians and Israelis together to build businesses, create jobs, and forge relationships".

"I have dedicated much of my life to building bridges between all people," Kraft said. "I believe deeply that all lives are worth protecting."

The owner of the Kraft Group, a sports and event management company, did not say whether he had rallied other stadium owners to ban Macklemore from their venues, as the rapper claims.

Macklemore - real name Benjamin Haggerty - called for a "free Palestine" and showed images of devastation in Gaza during two Sheeran concerts in New Jersey earlier this month.

GeneralTab.title: Interest rates hold expected but Bank of England facing tough choices
GeneralTab.text:
Policymakers at the Bank of England are expected to keep interest rates unchanged despite price rises accelerating due to the prolonged conflict in the Middle East.

The nine-member Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) has been meeting amid a backdrop of increasing global energy prices and interest rate rises around the world.

Economists expect the MPC to hold the benchmark Bank rate at 3.75% for a sixth consecutive meeting but analysts are more divided on whether the rate will need to go up before the end of the year.

The Bank rate is crucial in setting the benchmark for banks and other lenders in setting interest for individuals and businesses borrowing and saving money.

The latest interest rate decision will be announced by the Bank at 12:00 BST on Thursday.

Following its previous meeting at the end of July, the MPC indicated it could raise the Bank rate if the Iran war escalated.

Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey told the BBC at the time: "If we get a continuation of this conflict going on and oil prices stay above $100 a barrel... the odds are that interest rates will have to go up higher."

Oil prices moved above the $100 (£74) level on 9 September, and have remained there since, and there are few signs of a lasting truce in the Iran war.

The Bank uses interest rates to control inflation, which charts the rising cost of living. It aims to keep inflation at a target rate of 2%.

However, official figures released on Wednesday showed the Consumer Prices Index (CPI) measure of inflation had risen to 3.1% in August from 2.9% in July, pushing it to its highest rate in six months.

The acceleration was driven by rises in the cost of petrol, diesel and airfares.

Economists expect that higher global energy costs will feed through to food and fuel prices paid by consumers, meaning the inflation rate is yet to peak.

The MPC will be aware that, citing the Middle East conflict and warning inflation was "set to remain well above" its 2% target for some time, the European Central Bank recently raised interest rates to 2.5%.

In addition, the US Federal Reserve raised its interest rate to 3.5%-3.75% for similar reasons on Wednesday.

However, MPC members will also be keen not to put pressure on employers and further lower the prospects for those seeking a job.

Households feel the impact of a rising Bank rate through higher borrowing costs, but can benefit from more generous savings rates.

Given the global picture, and market expectations of a higher Bank rate, a host of major lenders have already increased the cost of new fixed-rate mortgages in recent days.

Andrew Montlake, chief executive of mortgage broker Coreco, said that the latest data showed that "the inflation dragon has not been fully slain".

"If inflation proves sticky, lenders' funding costs stay under pressure, which makes cheaper mortgages harder to deliver," he said.

"We are already seeing lenders reprice upwards, so this will do little to calm things down. Borrowers should not panic, but anyone approaching the end of a fixed rate should start looking early, secure an option and keep reviewing it."

The average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate is at its highest since 11 May, at 5.77%, while the average five-year is at its highest since 8 November 2023, at 5.83%, according to financial information service Moneyfacts.

Savers may be offered more generous returns, but the spending power of their savings could be eroded by the rising cost of living.

"It's almost impossible to time things just right, so I would urge households to focus on what's best for them now, in the medium term and in the longer term," said Harriet Guevara, chief savings officer at Nottingham Building Society.

"For savers, regularly check that your savings are earning a competitive return and that you have the right balance between easy access and money you can afford to put away for longer."

GeneralTab.title: US interest rates raised for first time in three years
GeneralTab.text:
US interest rates have been raised for the first time in more than three years and could be increased further in a bid to slow rising prices.

Rates were hiked to 3.75%-4% from 3.5%-3.75% by the Federal Reserve in a unanimous decision, despite fierce opposition from President Donald Trump, who had called for rates to be cut.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said the move was because "inflation is too high and has been for too long", adding that it was a "sober" and "responsible decision".

After the announcement, Trump expressed support for Warsh but said the Fed board, which votes on rate decisions, was "hostile".

Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for people wanting to secure loans, mortgages, and credit cards, but can lead to better returns on savings.

Warsh said during a press conference on Wednesday following the decision that, while there was "an attitude of optimism" within the Fed leadership, inflation remained a problem.

Like many central banks, the Fed has a target of keeping inflation at 2% or below. Warsh noted that US inflation has been above the target "for more than five years".

That has helped make affordability one of the top concerns of American voters, who have seen fuel prices surge in response to soaring wholesale oil prices since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran. This has driven up the cost of many goods and services, as well.

While the Fed "cannot affect any individual price – whether it be oil prices, whether it be food stuffs at the grocery store", Warsh said, the central bank can work to keep price rises from broadening across the economy.

He added that strength in the jobs market and wider economy meant the Fed was staying focused on stabilising prices, and that those least well off had the most to gain from lower inflation.

Central banks tend to increase rates when inflation is high to discourage spending and encourage saving, in the hope this will reduce the pace of price rises. But it's a balancing act, as higher rates can also encourage businesses to hold off on investing and hurt economic growth.

When he was confirmed, Democratic lawmakers had said Warsh would be Trump's "sock puppet" and many Fed watchers expected him to carry out Trump's persistent demands to slash rates. Trump had been heavily critical of Warsh's predecessor Jerome Powell for not cutting them.

Asked on Wednesday about the message the rate hike sent to Trump, Warsh chuckled before saying: "I have got nothing for you on a discussion with the president."

Trump told reporters later "I'm relying on Kevin [Warsh], but he's got, you know, a very tough board".

"And the, interest rates are too high. They're not appropriate... I talked to Kevin and I said, 'you might as well vote with the board because it's not going to matter.' The board is very hostile, they're very political," he added.

Earlier, Trump said on social media: "LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!"

Democrats on Capitol Hill said the rate increase would make loans costlier and, in turn, more Americans would go into debt.

"This is going to make everything become more expensive," said Chuck Schumer, the top Democrat in the Senate. "This is because Donald Trump does not know how to manage the economy."

The Fed's hike is the first rate move in any direction since they were cut in December 2025. The last time they were raised was in July 2023.

The increase could help push up mortgage rates for home buyers and lead to Americans paying more on other types of debt.

Major US banks JP Morgan, KeyCorp, and BNY all raised their prime lending rate on Wednesday to 7% from 6.75%, which will affect rates charged on credit cards and personal loans.

Mortgage costs have climbed over the past year but remain below peaks seen in 2023. A 30-year fixed deal is 6.76% on average, while a 15-year deal is 6.09%, according to figures from Freddie Mac.

Many US homeowners have 30-year and 15-year fixed-rate mortgages, and changes to interest rates will not impact their monthly repayments. But higher rates could affect those looking to secure a new mortgage or refinance.

Warsh declined to provide his own view on where he saw the Fed's rates going, but the majority of his fellow policymakers said they believe rates would be hiked again before the end of this year to between 4-4.25%.

A small majority also said rates could rise further to the 4.25-4.5% next year, before cuts begin in 2028 and 2029.

The forecast suggested price rises will ease in the coming years, with inflation, the measure used to assess the cost of living, predicted to fall steadily to the Fed's target by 2029.

The US Fed is not alone in facing rising inflation since the Iran war, with the European Central Bank raising rates last week and the Bank of England set to make its own decision on Thursday.

articles.title: Charles said Diana would be forgotten 'soon enough', Earl Spencer claims in book
articles.text:
Buckingham Palace has responded after a claim by Earl Spencer, the brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, that King Charles said "we'll forget her soon enough" days after her death.

Earl Spencer alleged the then-Prince of Wales subjected him to a "stream of anger" after he insisted Diana would not have wanted Princes William and Harry, then aged 15 and 12, to walk in her funeral procession.

The claim was made in an extract from his upcoming memoir, published by the Daily Mail.

A Palace spokesperson said: "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss."

Swan Song: Diana, My Sister is due to be published next week and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family. BBC News has not seen the book in full.

In the first extract, external from it to be made public, Earl Spencer claims to have been informed by a senior Palace aide that the young princes would walk alongside Princess Diana's coffin, which he objected to.

He claims to have received a phone call from Charles shortly after.

Earl Spencer wrote in the book: "He [Charles] unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death. 'Rest assured,' he hissed, 'we'll forget her soon enough'."

Earl Spencer's book about his sister seems set to open a very difficult time in the recent history of the Royal Family.

The death of Diana, a hugely popular figure, in a car crash in 1997, had created a volatile atmosphere, in which the royals were accused of failing to show feeling and empathy, and had seemed out of touch with the public mood.

Earl Spencer's emotional and defiant speech at her funeral added to that cloud of grievance hanging over Diana's untimely death.

Prince Harry has previously said that walking behind his mother's coffin aged 12 was something no child "should be asked to do".

In 2017, he told the BBC he didn't "have an opinion whether that was right or wrong", but "looking back on it", he was glad to have been part of the day.

Earlier on Wednesday, it emerged that copies of Earl Spencer's unreleased book had been stolen from a truck in the Netherlands.

BBC News understands four copies of the Dutch language edition were taken from a truck while it was en route from the Dutch publisher's printers to their warehouse.

articles.title: New hope for breast cancer patients as life-extending drug now on NHS in England
articles.text:
Patients in England with a specific type of incurable breast cancer can now access a life-extending drug on the NHS, two years after it was deemed too expensive by a health body.

Enhertu can give patients almost seven extra months to live on average - with some living up to three years longer.

Women in Scotland have had access to the drug on the NHS since 2023, and it is available in 26 other European countries.

Charities and patients have campaigned for it to be more widely available since 2024, when the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) said Enhertu was not good value for money.

From Thursday, doctors in England are now able to prescribe it, with Wales expected to follow shortly but the guidance doesn't automatically apply to Northern Ireland.

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said: "Enhertu can be life-changing, and this recommendation means NHS patients will finally be able to benefit from it.

"It is a tribute to the campaigners and charities who never stopped pressing for this."

This decision will affect about 1,000 women a year with a specific type of breast cancer, HER2-low.

Charity Breast Cancer Now said that while campaigners' "persistence paid off", thousands of people have missed out on access to Enhertu and many have died.

The charity's chief executive, Claire Rowney, said: "Today we can finally say we did it." However, she adds that "we can't celebrate this momentous decision without remembering the devastating cost of this delay".

Kate Wills, 51, understands this mix of emotions. She has HER2-low metastatic breast cancer, which has spread to her bones and lungs. But nothing about her suggests that she is terminally ill.

She has a high-powered job and is a wife and mum. Her social media feed shows a full and happy life - only the occasional medical appointment hints all is not well.

Kate says it has been "incredibly painful" to know that Enhertu could keep her alive for longer but she couldn't get it.

When she hears it will be available on the NHS, she immediately starts crying. "I really can't believe it. I'm so relieved, I'm overjoyed," she says.

"It's so hard keeping hope when you have stage four cancer. This gives me enormous hope."

Her son and daughter are in their teens and early 20s. Kate has been aiming to stay alive long enough for her youngest to finish school.

She smiles through her tears as she says: "Now I've just dared to dream that I might be around to see them fall in love, to get married."

For her, this is bittersweet. Her first thought is for "those women, my friends, who didn't get this in time".

The BBC understands that the drug companies Daiichi Sankyo and AstraZeneca have not substantially lowered their prices since the drug was first rejected.

The reason NICE has reversed its decision is largely because of a trade deal with the USA, where the UK government agreed to spend 25% more on medicines.

As part of this, NICE has increased how much the NHS will pay for every extra year of good quality life a medication can give.

This is known as a QALY (Quality-Adjusted Life Year) - and the upper threshold per QALY has gone from £30,000 to £35,000.

At the end of August, NICE also introduced a different, more nuanced, way of measuring a patient's quality of life.

These two changes were enough to tip the balance.

It is thought that patient campaigns for Enhertu - and other drugs - have helped too.

Daiichi Sankyo and AstraZeneca welcome NICE's decision, but the latter is calling for "strong collaboration" across the healthcare system to ensure "faster, more equitable patient access in the future".

Breast Cancer Now's Claire Rowney says: "We are calling on the government, NICE, NHS England and the pharmaceutical industry to work together to fix this broken system, so that people with incurable metastatic breast cancer are not forced to spend precious months and years campaigning for treatments that could give them more time."

Helen Knight, director of medicines evaluation at NICE, says she is pleased a "commercial solution" means the treatment can be made available on the NHS in England but adds she knows the decision "comes too late for many families".

"Our role is important in ensuring NHS spending on new medicines reflects the benefits they deliver while protecting valuable health resources for other essential patient services," she says.

For Kate, the thought of dying before she had to, "when there was a drug that I just could almost reach but couldn't get", was "so incredibly painful".

"To know that I can get it now is absolutely everything."

articles.title: Robert Kraft says Ed Sheeran asked him to donate $2m to aid after Macklemore backlash
articles.text:
The US stadium owner who had pro-Palestinian rapper Macklemore removed as Ed Sheeran's opening act at his venue says Sheeran has asked him to donate $2m to "aid in the region".

New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft announced the requested pledge in his second statement this week on the controversy, without specifying where exactly the funds would go.

Kraft confirmed on Monday he had Macklemore dropped as opening act from Sheeran's forthcoming Loop Tour at the Gillette Stadium near Boston, accusing the rapper of hate speech.

Facing a backlash, Sheeran has said the decision to drop Macklemore was made by promoters and that he would not be drawn into a public debate over Gaza.

On Wednesday, Macklemore said he would donate $1m to Palestinian organisations, challenging Kraft to match the sum.

In a statement later that day, Kraft, 85, said: "Earlier today, before Macklemore challenged me to match his donation, Ed called me and asked me to commit $2 million to match his donation to aid in the region to fight this humanitarian crisis.

"Ed now plans to reach out to other venue owners and our goal is to continue to work together to build bridges."

In the statement, which was issued by Gillette Stadium on Kraft's behalf, he said he would like those speaking in support of the Palestinian people to know that he has long "supported efforts that create opportunity for Palestinians".

He also said that he has worked to bring "young Palestinians and Israelis together to build businesses, create jobs, and forge relationships".

"I have dedicated much of my life to building bridges between all people," Kraft said. "I believe deeply that all lives are worth protecting."

The owner of the Kraft Group, a sports and event management company, did not say whether he had rallied other stadium owners to ban Macklemore from their venues, as the rapper claims.

Macklemore - real name Benjamin Haggerty - called for a "free Palestine" and showed images of devastation in Gaza during two Sheeran concerts in New Jersey earlier this month.

He was dropped on Monday from Sheeran's line-up, just days before the tour was set to resume in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, on Saturday.

Sheeran, who performed at Kraft's 2022 wedding, said on Tuesday he was not responsible for Macklemore being removed as an opening act from the tour.

articles.title: UK weather: At least seven months of relentless rain needed to end drought in England
articles.text:
Above-average rainfall is needed across England for the next seven months for all areas to recover from drought by spring 2027, according to new research.

The Environment Agency (EA) stated that despite some wet weather during the first half of September, almost three-quarters of England remains in drought following an exceptionally dry spring and summer as well as a succession of heatwaves.

It says around 120% of typical rainfall is needed between now and April for all areas to be considered out of drought.

Even under the most likely rainfall scenario - which predicts a wetter autumn than normal based on the latest Met Office forecasts - Devon and Cornwall and East Anglia could still be in drought by the start of spring 2027.

Other predictions suggest there is also roughly a one-in-four chance that around half of England will still be in drought next spring, but currently only a 1% chance of a severe drought in the coming months.

The EA defines severe drought as a situation where water shortages have extensive and lasting impacts on the environment, farming, communities and the economy, and where there may be a serious threat to public water supplies. England has not seen a severe drought since 1976.

Recent rain has brought some relief, however, groundwater levels remain low and reservoir storage across England stood at just under 57% last week, around a fifth below the level normally expected at this time of year.

EA Chief Executive Philip Duffy said: "The drought situation remains very serious, and we cannot underestimate the challenge ahead over the coming months.

"A few weeks of rain cannot reverse the deficit we face from the very dry spring and summer. We still need everyone to use a little less water to speed up the drought recovery."

In Scotland the recent rainfall has not yet reversed the impact of months of dry conditions around parts of its east coast, with four areas now at significant water scarcity whilst the whole of Wales also remains in drought status.

Significant water scarcity is declared when river flows remain below the recognised low flow threshold for 30 consecutive days.

Although there is some rain in the short-range forecast, it is unlikely to be the kind of prolonged amount needed to alleviate the dry conditions over much of the UK.

Thursday will start off with some rain across south-eastern areas of England, taking some time to clear away from the Kent coast.

Sunny spells will develop elsewhere with some showers, especially across Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England.

With an area of low pressure situated to the north of Scotland, there will also be some blustery conditions across the UK.

articles.title: Snapchat open to putting time limits on teens, boss tells BBC
articles.text:
The boss of Snapchat-parent Snap Inc says the firm would be "willing to implement" time limits for teens, following a call from Meta for it to take action.

Evan Spiegel told the BBC in an interview at the company's California headquarters that setting a maximum amount of time that young users could spend on the app could be "an important step forward for the industry."

His comments came as Snap revealed a slew of new features for its upcoming Specs glasses, which it said could connect to Apple iPhone and Mac devices.

Meta has been pressuring other social media companies to join it in making platform changes it agreed to as part of a recent multi-billion dollar legal settlement with US states.

Instagram and Facebook-parent Meta was facing allegations from Attorneys General for most US states who said the firm deliberately designed its apps to be addictive to young users.

It agreed to pay $12.7bn and implement a two-hour daily limit for teen users across its platforms by default, in addition to muted notifications during school hours, blocks at night and other measures.

"I think it is an important step forward in the industry in terms of really identifying industry norms, and I think that would be beneficial overall," Spiegel told the BBC. "We've looked really thoughtfully at the terms."

As part of Meta's August settlement, the company said it would implement even more stringent time limits and pay an additional $5.3bn if YouTube and TikTok follow suit. It has denied any wrongdoing as part of the deal, which will be paid over a 10-year period.

Last month, a Meta spokesperson said it was hopeful that Snap would make similar platform changes as well.

Meta, YouTube, TikTok and Snap have all faced a barrage of litigation alleging their apps have helped spawn a youth mental health crisis. Snap has also been accused of facilitating illegal drug sales.

When asked about the idea of a default time limit, Spiegel said: "I think that's a really good example of something that that we'd be willing to implement."

But Spiegel did not commit to a timeline on when Snap might take action.

"That's something we've talked about internally," he said. "I don't have more to share today."

He noted that Snap offers tools through its Family Center feature, which currently enables parents to track aspects of how their teens are using Snapchat.

"We want to figure out how we can be part of the solution," Spiegel added.

YouTube-parent Google said it had no comment when asked if it planned to implement the measures in Meta's settlement. TikTok did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

With the device, Snap aims to offer a middle ground between VR headsets like Meta's Quest 3 and lightweight AI smart glasses offered by rivals which look more like conventional glasses.

"We're creating a totally new category here," said Spiegel.

"You have a really powerful computer that brings a lot of the immersive capability you see with VR, but they're also lightweight at just about 130 grams, so they're very wearable and they have these see-through lenses, so you can use them out in the world."

Specs is Snap's most recent foray into the wearable tech, coming a decade after its short-lived Spectacles cost the company tens of millions of dollars.

The device is also arriving as Meta is facing a significant backlash over its own smart glasses, which are estimated to be the most popular of the market.

Some online derisively call them "pervert glasses" over how they have been used to secretly film women, with one person telling the BBC they were filmed leaving the beach, while another said they were told to pay to remove a video of them from the internet.

Nevertheless, sales continue to rise. With seven million pairs having been sold according to Meta.

Snap said it has built into the design of Specs, which do not use facial recognition to identify people.

A white light flashes at the top of the glasses above the users nose when it is recording video and taking a photo.

The company says that will let people nearby see that recording is happening.

Users of Meta glasses have figured out ways to obscure components meant to indicate that a photo or video is being captured, including by tampering with the electronics in the device.

Meta says it has remotely disabled the cameras on thousands of its devices on which tampering or destruction of the indicator light was detected.

articles.title: Body found in search for missing Suffolk boy Noah Woods, 3
articles.text:
A body has been found in the search for missing three-year-old boy Noah Woods, police have confirmed.

Noah disappeared at about 15:00 BST on Tuesday from a playground in Brantham, Suffolk, after becoming separated from a relative.

Supt Tom Pearse of Suffolk Police said dive teams recovered the body of a child from a nearby pond.

He said the death was being treated as unexplained but not suspicious.

Supt Pearse said formal identification had yet to take place, but Noah's family had been informed.

"Our thoughts are with Noah's family and all those who knew him," he said.

"We have been overwhelmed by the outpouring of public support and people putting on their boots to help."

Police said at least 1,300 members of the public had helped in the search for the missing boy, who was non-verbal and partially deaf.

People from as far afield as Birmingham and Hampshire had turned up to help.

Helicopters, dog units and members of the public had been scouring the area, close to the estuary of the River Stour on the Essex border.

Volunteer efforts had been co-ordinated from Brantham Leisure Centre and the village hall, which ran out of hi-vis vests due to the number of volunteers.

Those looking for Noah had been told he would not respond to shouting.

Michael Crowley, who was working opposite the playground on Tuesday and was one of the last people to see Noah before he went missing, said: "He looked happy and healthy as anything."

Jessica Gammons, a mother-of-two from Kelvedon, in Essex, was among the many volunteers who went out to look for the toddler.

She said she felt compelled join the search, despite being heavily pregnant, because her son, like Noah, is three years old.

"I kept thinking to myself 'If this was my son, I'd want everyone possible to help,'" she said.

"It's such a sad situation. I can't stop thinking about him."

Supt Pearse continued: "Since Noah was reported as missing, a vast number of our officers and staff have been deployed in numerous functions in the search for Noah and support for his family.

"We've been supported by Suffolk HART (Hazardous Area Response Team), SULSAR (Suffolk Lowland Search and Rescue), Environment Agency, HM Coastguard, Fire and Rescue Service and the ambulance service.

"As a parent myself, I completely understand why people would want to help and such a response is one that typifies the strong sense of community and the heart-warming nature of Suffolk people that make the county such a special place.

"I am sure you appreciate the family now need time, space and privacy and I thank you for your understanding in this."

articles.title: UK prosecutors file for extradition of the Tate brothers from the US
articles.text:
Prosecutors in the UK have lodged a formal request for the extradition of brothers Andrew and Tristan Tate from the US to face charges of rape and sex trafficking.

The US State Department, which received the requests last week, will review the extradition applications to make sure they comply with the existing agreement between the US and UK.

But the lawyer for the brothers, who are dual US-UK citizens, accused British authorities of failing to provide the necessary supporting documents in the request.

The brothers are facing a total of 59 charges in the UK, including rape and counts relating to sex trafficking and indecent images of a child. Both men deny any wrongdoing.

The Crown Prosecution Service originally brought 21 charges, but added 38 more in July for alleged actions spanning between 2010 and 2017.

US authorities took the men into custody in July after the UK announced the new charges. The brothers lost a bid to be released from a Florida jail on bail last week.

UK authorities had until Wednesday 16 September to submit a full extradition request.

Joe McBride, the brothers' lawyer, said he would be challenging the requests, arguing they were not backed up by the information needed under the extradition agreement.

In a statement to the BBC, McBride said the brothers had also not received the extradition requests themselves, nor documents such as "a warrant, a charging document, and information that provides a reasonable basis to believe my clients committed these offences".

"This cloak-and-dagger act speaks to the deception behind these accusations and to their weakness," he added.

Once the State Department completes it review, there are still several legal steps before extradition can be permitted. Applications must go through the US Justice Department which will in turn forward it to the court, where the final decision on their extradition will be made.

During this legal process, the Tate brothers will remain in jail in the US.

An official letter from the State Department details that Andrew Tate, 39, is "wanted to stand trial in the United Kingdom" on a series of charges, including 10 counts of rape, three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation and three counts of assault occasioning actual bodily harm.

He is also accused of making and distributing indecent images of a child and possessing extreme pornography.

Charges levelled against Tristan Tate, 38, include five counts of rape, six counts of assault occasioning actual bodily harm, three counts of sex trafficking and a sexual assault.

Both men deny any wrongdoing.

In response to the formal request for extradition from the US, a Home Office spokesperson said: "As a matter of long-standing policy and practice, we do not routinely comment on individual cases."

The former professional kickboxers turned divisive social media influencers hold dual US and British citizenship, and had primarily been living in Romania since 2017.

They have been accused of promoting misogyny and toxic masculinity online, which has attracted a large following, particularly from young men.

Andrew Tate, who is a self-proclaimed "misogynist", first rose to fame after a 2016 appearance on the British version of reality TV show Big Brother.

The brothers also faced sex-trafficking charges in Romania in 2022, and were under a travel ban until they were allowed to come to the US in 2025.

Both brothers have denied all charges and allegations.

articles.title: Two Britons among three killed in Swiss Alps light aircraft crash
articles.text:
Two Britons are among three people killed in a plane crash in the Swiss Alps.

The light aircraft crashed high in the mountains near the town of Leukerbad in the southern canton of Valais on Tuesday.

The authorities said the Cirrus SR22T took off from Sion airport in the Rhône Valley and, for unknown reasons, collided with a mountain slope about 10 minutes later.

Witnesses reported seeing a fire and smoke.

Emergency teams from the Valais Rescue Organisation, police and firefighters were sent to the scene along with three helicopters.

The Swiss Transportation Safety Board has started an investigation.

And the Valais Police and the Office of the Attorney General have launched a inquiry.

Formal identification of the victims is under way.

The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) confirmed it was "providing support to the families of two British nationals who died in Switzerland".

It said officials were in contact with the local authorities.

"Our thoughts remain with the families during this difficult time," it added.

articles.title: Photos show widespread damage at US sites from Iranian attacks
articles.text:
Images showing widespread damage to multiple US sites in the Middle East from Iranian strikes have been obtained by the BBC's US partner CBS.

The photos, provided by active military personnel, show a severed radar jet, flattened trailers and severely damaged buildings.

The undated photos were taken at US bases and sites in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait.

One member of the military, who was not named by CBS, said: "This is major damage to our bases that hasn't been communicated to the American public.

"We're standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face."

The White House referred the BBC to US Central Command. Centcom did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The photos, which have not been independently verified by the BBC, were published the day after a report from the Pentagon's watchdog confirmed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in the Middle East have been damaged and destroyed by Iran.

One of the photos showed a destroyed Boeing E-3 Sentry at Prince Sultan Air Force Base in Saudi Arabia that has been ripped in half, its tail section crumpled into a tangled mess of metal.

While the photo is undated, BBC Verify previously confirmed a similar photo, apparently of the same radar aircraft in March.

The Boeing E-3 Awacs are used to detect and track potential targets at long ranges to provide an early warning of possible threats.

At the time, a US official told Reuters that 12 US personnel had been wounded, two of them seriously, in an Iranian attack on the air base.

A pair of undated images reportedly from Camp Beuhring, Kuwait, show crumpled trailers, and a large tent-like structure that had been reduced to shreds as smoke billowed from the site.

Another image shows a four-storey building damaged by an Iranian strike at Camp Arifjan, in Kuwait.

Damage to the site was reported in March, including on satellite communications hardware, though it is not clear whether this image is from the same attack.

Brian Katulis, a former national security official under both Democratic and Republican administrations, said that the damage visible in the images showed that "America had not adequately prepared its defences".

"And there is strong evidence that US adversaries like China and Russia may have helped Iran in targeting," added Katulis, now a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute. "The Trump administration has done nothing to address these vulnerabilities."

The images were published on the heels of a report from the Pentagon's watchdog, which found Iranian strikes had "damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan during the conflict".

It also noted that equipment losses have totalled $3.7bn (£2.8bn). Overall, the US spent $33.4bn (£24.7bn) on the war up to 29 June, the report said.

In the months after the war began, "dozens of US aircraft were destroyed or damaged", the report continues.

The document lists several of the aircraft damaged, including five refuelling aircraft which were "damaged or destroyed on the ground in Saudi Arabia by Iranian munitions".

A separate report , externalfrom the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) notes that the E-3 aircraft is no longer in production and would have to be replaced with a more modern equivalent, the E-7.

The CBO noted that the E-3 aircraft alone costs $500m (£371m), and the estimated total cost of equipment lost in battle - including planes, drones and a terminal high altitude area defence system - amounts to $1.9b (£1.4b).

CBO said that its review was subject to "uncertainty" because the defence department did not respond to its requests for information, requiring the agency to rely on government databases and public reports.

Additionally, the extent of repairs and rebuilding that the US military plans to do remains unclear, according to the report.

Brian Katulis of the Middle East Institute said that while "these costs show how the Trump administration burned through precious military resources without having much to show for it", the greater damage had been to broader US military readiness.

"The United States had to divert military assets from Asia to the Middle East, leaving America and its partners in Asia more exposed and vulnerable to China," he said.

"In addition, the depletion of US munitions makes Russia more willing to probe vulnerabilities with America's NATO allies and continue its aggressive war against Ukraine."

While the US has the financial resources to address the equipment losses, it is already facing budgetary problems and may not be able to do so fast enough to prepare for potential flare-ups in the Middle East or elsewhere in the world, he added.

Public and political pressure has mounted on the White House to find an end to the conflict with Iran, which began on 28 February when the US and Israel launched joint attacks on the country.

Since the war began Iran has repeatedly attacked US bases and allied states in the Gulf, as well as Israel.

On Tuesday night, the US House of Representatives voted for the third time to end the war in Iran, approving a measure that would force President Donald Trump to end US military action without congressional approval.

The vote passed with the help of several Republicans, in what could be the final House vote on the matter ahead of the US midterm elections in November.

It faces an uncertain path to passage - the US Senate has not indicated if it will take up the matter.

The same day, outgoing Republican Congressman Thomas Massie announced an attempt to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth as new details emerged about the Iran war's price tag for the US.

The Trump administration backed Hegseth, with US attorney general Todd Blanche telling reporters he was "doing a phenomenal job".

articles.title: EU chief backs plan for Canada to become 'associate member'
articles.text:
The president of the European Commission has backed proposals for Canada to become the EU's first "associate member".

Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament on Wednesday she wanted to work on "opening the door" for Canada, which would involve closer ties on various key sectors.

The country currently faces tense relations with the US, compounded by an intensifying dispute over trade.

Insisting it would not be a "partnership against anyone else", Von der Leyen did not mention Donald Trump by name. Nevertheless the US president threatened to cut trade with the European Union in response to the proposal.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney last week spoke of seeking a "unique alliance" with the EU.

Carney was in attendance at the annual key note speech in Strasbourg, and is due to address the parliament on Thursday.

Trade talks between Canada and the US collapsed last month, sparking a series of new tariff measures. Trump's repeated talk of making Canada a "51st state" has also helped to fuel the feud between the North American neighbours.

Von der Leyen told the EU's State of the Union address that the bloc and Canada "see the world with the same eyes", including on topics ranging from AI, to climate change and geopolitics.

"And we have stood together: on Ukraine, on defence, on raw materials and on supply chains. But above all... Europe and Canada believe in democracy."

She added: "Partnerships are a strategic choice for Europe. But they also respond to the fracture in the international rules-based system".

She did not give specific details on how any Canadian membership would work, but listed manufacturing, technology, artificial intelligence (AI), defence, energy, critical minerals and economic security as key areas for cooperation.

When asked about the plan, Trump called it "laughable".

"If they do that, if I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe, on many things."

He added: "If it's a good intention, that's fine. If it's a bad intention, we'll put very heavy tariffs on Europe, which is a possibility."

Both von der Leyen and other European leaders have found a reliable ally in Carney as they deal with similar problems.

In particular, they have faced Trump's aggressive use of tariffs and his threat to annex Greenland which is a sovereign territory of EU member Denmark.

But "associate membership" of the EU does not currently exist and the process, if agreed, could take years.

Earlier this year, Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz suggested - to a mixed reaction - that Ukraine could be granted this new status.

Some countries in the western Balkans including Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia, and Serbia are already on the long road towards full EU membership.

In Eastern Europe, Georgia and Moldova are also applying.

Ten of the bloc's 27 members are yet to ratify a free-trade agreement struck with Ottawa nearly a decade ago, and some capitals would prefer to build on existing defence and trade agreements rather than create a new form of membership for Canada.

Setting out the EU's political and policy priorities for the year ahead, von der Leyen also proposed the formation of a European Security Council, which would include the UK and Ukraine, amid an ongoing threat to the continent from Russia.

"For a long time, we have discussed a leaders' format focused on the security of our continent, with partners like Canada, Norway, Ukraine, the United Kingdom and others involved," she said in the wide-ranging address.

"This is even more urgent now, given the nature and scale of the risks at play. This is why we will set out our ideas to make a European Security Council a reality."

Calls for such a body have been growing since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

It was initially a French-German conception but more countries have shown support, particularly as Trump has questioned the Nato military alliance. Other nations worry such a council could unhelpfully rival Nato.

Von der Leyen said the EU was "strengthening our work with Nato" and that expanded defence spending would be "fully aligned" with the alliance.

But at the core of such a security council would be the ability to trigger an emergency meeting if one member felt under threat, similar to Nato's Article 4.

The EU chief said it would be a "mechanism to flank" Article 4, a term that could be interpreted as complementing Nato functions or - if taken in a military context - bypassing them.

Alongside global threats, von der Leyen also said many European families were worried about the cost of living, and the "dizzying speed of change" of technology and its impacts on jobs and society.

Other proposals included inviting the world's largest AI labs for talks on how to support industry efforts to pace the frontier, as well as slashing bureaucracy for businesses in the EU.

Plans to curb social media use among children, including banning platforms for under 13s, were also put forward. Under the proposal, children aged 13 to 15 would only be able to set up social media accounts which are supervised by parents.

A new emergency tool to help countries better deal with mass migration movements following the deadly influx of migrants to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in July would also be outlined.

The pledge chimes with the message of European politicians on the right and hard right who have gained support in recent years for proposing a tougher approach.

Some of them called the mass attempt to enter the EU through Ceuta an "invasion" and argued asylum rules should be suspended to deal with such a crisis.

Von der Leyen said the new emergency tool would "only be triggered under a strictly defined set of criteria" and for a specific period of time, and that fundamental rights would be protected.

Human rights groups worry such a move would see vulnerable people, including women and children, turned back and denied the protection afforded to them under international law.

articles.title: US House votes to hold billionaire Epstein associate Leon Black in contempt of Congress
articles.text:
The US House of Representatives has agreed to hold billionaire Leon Black in contempt of Congress for defying a legal summons related to its investigation into convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Black, who had business ties to Epstein, did not comply with a subpoena ordering him to appear before the House Oversight Committee earlier this month and share documents related to Epstein.

Lawyers for Black, who has sued over the summons, called the contempt move "outrageous".

After passage of the measure holding Black in contempt, Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer said: "No-one is above the law. We will continue to seek transparency for the American people and justice for survivors."

In a statement shared with US media, lawyers for Black called the House move an "outrageous action that ignores the facts and the truth about Mr Black".

"The full House is holding him in contempt without any regard to the active litigation challenging the lawfulness of the Committee's actions and the ethics complaint against Chairman Comer," they said.

The measure, which passed by unanimous consent, means the matter will be referred to the US justice department, which will decide whether to criminally prosecute Black.

In a written statement, the committee's top Democrat, congressman Robert Garcia, called the contempt vote "an important step towards justice and accountability".

"We will continue to center the survivors in our fight to hold those responsible for these horrific crimes," he said.

The private equity tycoon walked out of voluntary testimony before the House Oversight Committee in June after he was asked about nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) he may have signed, lawmakers said at the time.

Black left Apollo Global Management, which he co-founded, amid scrutiny in 2021 over his Epstein ties. He has denied any wrongdoing with regards to his dealings with Epstein.

The subpoenas, which ordered Black to share NDAs and give an on-camera deposition under oath, were issued after he left the committee meeting in June.

Black has said he hired Epstein as a wealth management adviser, telling lawmakers in June that he gave Epstein $158m (£118m) for legitimate reasons.

The billionaire has said he did not know about Epstein's crimes until he was charged with sex trafficking in July 2019.

articles.title: At least 21 killed after war-damaged Gaza building collapses
articles.text:
At least 21 people have been killed, including eight children, after a war-damaged building collapsed in the Gaza Strip overnight, rescuers and medics say.

Witnesses told the BBC that the six-storey building in Gaza City's Tal al-Hawa area had been left tilting dangerously to one side after an Israeli strike more than a year ago. Displaced families had lived inside because they were desperate, they said.

UN and Egyptian teams joined the search for survivors, which was slow due to a lack of equipment. Initially, rescuers from the Hamas-run Civil Defence agency had to use their bare hands.

On Wednesday afternoon, they said they had ended the operation after taking 45 injured people to hospitals.

Sherif, whose sister was killed, said: "They couldn't find a tent or somewhere to live.

"This was the last place they could turn to, despite the danger. They were aware that it would likely end in tragedy. A lack of resources drove them towards certain death."

A woman living in a tent nearby, Umm Mohammed Bakrun, said she had been talking to her son when the building collapsed suddenly in the early hours of Wednesday.

"It felt like an earthquake. There was a loud sound and I couldn't stand up. Stones rained down on us and when I looked outside I saw a lot of dust," she told the BBC. "Within minutes, there were screams everywhere."

Another witness, Mansour Abu Mohammed, said the building collapsed "in a few seconds".

"Every day, a stone or a few stones would fall from it, but the people inside couldn't find anywhere else to live. I used to live next door to it and you could see that it was tilting to one side."

Satellite imagery shows that the area around the building was targeted in the early weeks of the war, while damage to the building itself first became evident in 2024.

The head of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) Gaza office, Alessandro Mrakic, told reporters at the scene on Wednesday morning that "the situation... is tragic because we don't have the equipment and machinery that is needed".

He also warned that approximately 400 other war-damaged buildings across Gaza were at imminent risk of collapse, particularly as winter approaches.

"We need support, most importantly with machinery, equipment, among others. Our colleagues here don't have [engine] oil and spare parts to continue to work with all the equipment that is still in Gaza."

The UN's humanitarian relief co-ordinator, Ramiz Alakbarov, said he was "devastated" by the reports of the building collapse.

"No-one should have to risk their life simply to find a safe place to shelter," he said.

He also urged Israeli authorities to approve deliveries to Gaza of heavy machinery for rescue operations, as well as tents, tarpaulins and other non-food items for displaced people ahead of the winter rains.

Israel says its restrictions are meant to keep equipment out of the hands of Palestinian armed groups that could also have military uses.

An estimated 80% of all structures in Gaza have been destroyed or damaged during the war between Israel and Hamas, according to the UN.

More than 1.9 million people - about 90% of the territory's population - have been displaced, many of them multiple times, and 1.2 million of them are currently living in tents or makeshift shelters, it says.

The UN has warned that the humanitarian situation in Gaza remains dire despite the ceasefire agreed last October, as Israeli air strikes and other attacks continue to hit populated areas, causing casualties and property damage and driving further displacement.

On Tuesday, Israeli air strikes killed at least five Palestinians, including two children and a Hamas commander, according to health officials and Hamas sources.

The Israeli military said it killed a Hamas commander in southern Gaza and another fighter in the north. In both cases, a child was also reportedly killed.

Separately, the British charity Medical Aid for Palestinians said that a patient was killed by an Israeli drone at a health centre it supports in Jabalia in northern Gaza. A spokesperson for the Israeli military told the BBC it was not aware of such an incident.

The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 73,790 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

articles.title: Interest rates hold expected but Bank of England facing tough choices
articles.text:
Policymakers at the Bank of England are expected to keep interest rates unchanged despite price rises accelerating due to the prolonged conflict in the Middle East.

The nine-member Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) has been meeting amid a backdrop of increasing global energy prices and interest rate rises around the world.

Economists expect the MPC to hold the benchmark Bank rate at 3.75% for a sixth consecutive meeting but analysts are more divided on whether the rate will need to go up before the end of the year.

The Bank rate is crucial in setting the benchmark for banks and other lenders in setting interest for individuals and businesses borrowing and saving money.

The latest interest rate decision will be announced by the Bank at 12:00 BST on Thursday.

Following its previous meeting at the end of July, the MPC indicated it could raise the Bank rate if the Iran war escalated.

Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey told the BBC at the time: "If we get a continuation of this conflict going on and oil prices stay above $100 a barrel... the odds are that interest rates will have to go up higher."

Oil prices moved above the $100 (£74) level on 9 September, and have remained there since, and there are few signs of a lasting truce in the Iran war.

The Bank uses interest rates to control inflation, which charts the rising cost of living. It aims to keep inflation at a target rate of 2%.

However, official figures released on Wednesday showed the Consumer Prices Index (CPI) measure of inflation had risen to 3.1% in August from 2.9% in July, pushing it to its highest rate in six months.

The acceleration was driven by rises in the cost of petrol, diesel and airfares.

Economists expect that higher global energy costs will feed through to food and fuel prices paid by consumers, meaning the inflation rate is yet to peak.

The MPC will be aware that, citing the Middle East conflict and warning inflation was "set to remain well above" its 2% target for some time, the European Central Bank recently raised interest rates to 2.5%.

In addition, the US Federal Reserve raised its interest rate to 3.5%-3.75% for similar reasons on Wednesday.

However, MPC members will also be keen not to put pressure on employers and further lower the prospects for those seeking a job.

Households feel the impact of a rising Bank rate through higher borrowing costs, but can benefit from more generous savings rates.

Given the global picture, and market expectations of a higher Bank rate, a host of major lenders have already increased the cost of new fixed-rate mortgages in recent days.

Andrew Montlake, chief executive of mortgage broker Coreco, said that the latest data showed that "the inflation dragon has not been fully slain".

"If inflation proves sticky, lenders' funding costs stay under pressure, which makes cheaper mortgages harder to deliver," he said.

"We are already seeing lenders reprice upwards, so this will do little to calm things down. Borrowers should not panic, but anyone approaching the end of a fixed rate should start looking early, secure an option and keep reviewing it."

The average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate is at its highest since 11 May, at 5.77%, while the average five-year is at its highest since 8 November 2023, at 5.83%, according to financial information service Moneyfacts.

Savers may be offered more generous returns, but the spending power of their savings could be eroded by the rising cost of living.

"It's almost impossible to time things just right, so I would urge households to focus on what's best for them now, in the medium term and in the longer term," said Harriet Guevara, chief savings officer at Nottingham Building Society.

"For savers, regularly check that your savings are earning a competitive return and that you have the right balance between easy access and money you can afford to put away for longer."

articles.title: US interest rates raised for first time in three years
articles.text:
US interest rates have been raised for the first time in more than three years and could be increased further in a bid to slow rising prices.

Rates were hiked to 3.75%-4% from 3.5%-3.75% by the Federal Reserve in a unanimous decision, despite fierce opposition from President Donald Trump, who had called for rates to be cut.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said the move was because "inflation is too high and has been for too long", adding that it was a "sober" and "responsible decision".

After the announcement, Trump expressed support for Warsh but said the Fed board, which votes on rate decisions, was "hostile".

Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for people wanting to secure loans, mortgages, and credit cards, but can lead to better returns on savings.

Warsh said during a press conference on Wednesday following the decision that, while there was "an attitude of optimism" within the Fed leadership, inflation remained a problem.

Like many central banks, the Fed has a target of keeping inflation at 2% or below. Warsh noted that US inflation has been above the target "for more than five years".

That has helped make affordability one of the top concerns of American voters, who have seen fuel prices surge in response to soaring wholesale oil prices since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran. This has driven up the cost of many goods and services, as well.

While the Fed "cannot affect any individual price – whether it be oil prices, whether it be food stuffs at the grocery store", Warsh said, the central bank can work to keep price rises from broadening across the economy.

He added that strength in the jobs market and wider economy meant the Fed was staying focused on stabilising prices, and that those least well off had the most to gain from lower inflation.

Central banks tend to increase rates when inflation is high to discourage spending and encourage saving, in the hope this will reduce the pace of price rises. But it's a balancing act, as higher rates can also encourage businesses to hold off on investing and hurt economic growth.

When he was confirmed, Democratic lawmakers had said Warsh would be Trump's "sock puppet" and many Fed watchers expected him to carry out Trump's persistent demands to slash rates. Trump had been heavily critical of Warsh's predecessor Jerome Powell for not cutting them.

Asked on Wednesday about the message the rate hike sent to Trump, Warsh chuckled before saying: "I have got nothing for you on a discussion with the president."

Trump told reporters later "I'm relying on Kevin [Warsh], but he's got, you know, a very tough board".

"And the, interest rates are too high. They're not appropriate... I talked to Kevin and I said, 'you might as well vote with the board because it's not going to matter.' The board is very hostile, they're very political," he added.

Earlier, Trump said on social media: "LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!"

Democrats on Capitol Hill said the rate increase would make loans costlier and, in turn, more Americans would go into debt.

"This is going to make everything become more expensive," said Chuck Schumer, the top Democrat in the Senate. "This is because Donald Trump does not know how to manage the economy."

The Fed's hike is the first rate move in any direction since they were cut in December 2025. The last time they were raised was in July 2023.

The increase could help push up mortgage rates for home buyers and lead to Americans paying more on other types of debt.

Major US banks JP Morgan, KeyCorp, and BNY all raised their prime lending rate on Wednesday to 7% from 6.75%, which will affect rates charged on credit cards and personal loans.

Mortgage costs have climbed over the past year but remain below peaks seen in 2023. A 30-year fixed deal is 6.76% on average, while a 15-year deal is 6.09%, according to figures from Freddie Mac.

Many US homeowners have 30-year and 15-year fixed-rate mortgages, and changes to interest rates will not impact their monthly repayments. But higher rates could affect those looking to secure a new mortgage or refinance.

Warsh declined to provide his own view on where he saw the Fed's rates going, but the majority of his fellow policymakers said they believe rates would be hiked again before the end of this year to between 4-4.25%.

A small majority also said rates could rise further to the 4.25-4.5% next year, before cuts begin in 2028 and 2029.

The forecast suggested price rises will ease in the coming years, with inflation, the measure used to assess the cost of living, predicted to fall steadily to the Fed's target by 2029.

The US Fed is not alone in facing rising inflation since the Iran war, with the European Central Bank raising rates last week and the Bank of England set to make its own decision on Thursday.
