articles.title: Olu Jacobs: Legendary Nollywood actor dies in Nigeria aged 84
articles.text:
Olu Jacobs, one of Nigeria's best known actors, whose career spanned several decades across theatre, television and film, has died at the age of 84.

His wife, veteran actress Joke Silva, announced his death and asked for privacy while the family mourns.

Silva announced his passing in a statement describing the celebrated actor as "The Lion of Lufodo" and saying his life was "well lived and fought".

Some of his notable films include My Kingdom, Covert Operation and One Fine Day.

He was regarded as one of the father figures of Nollywood, as Nigeria's film industry in known, commanding widespread respect and admiration across the country.

"We call on all bloggers and social media influencers to respect our family's privacy at this time," Silva said in a statement.

Born on 11 July 1942, Jacobs was trained at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London before embarking on a career that included appearances in British television productions and international films.

He became one of the defining figures of Nigeria's film industry, appearing in numerous Nigerian productions and earning recognition for his commanding screen presence and versatility.

His career spanned more than five decades, during which he received several major honours, including the African Movie Academy Award for Best Actor in a Leading Role and lifetime achievement honours.

In 2011, Jacobs was conferred with the national honour of Member of the Order of the Federal Republic (MFR) in recognition of his contribution to the Nigerian film industry.

Jacobs and Silva jointly established the Lufodo Group and Lufodo Academy of Performing Arts, contributing not only to film and television but also to developing and training performing artists in Nigeria.

In recent years, Jacobs had largely stayed away from the public spotlight due to ill-health.

In 2021, Silva disclosed that he had been diagnosed with Dementia with Lewy bodies.

"It's a degenerative disease that affects the brain and it's almost like a Parkinson-type of disease - it affects the brain and affects the person," she said in an interview with Nigerian broadcaster Chude Jideonwo.

On several occasions, there were rumours that Jacobs had died, but his family would promptly debunk them, the latest being in June 2024 when his eldest son, Soji, went on TV to say his father was still alive.

articles.title: Emmys remember Catherine O'Hara, Rob Reiner and Hayden Panettiere
articles.text:
Macaulay Culkin, Annie Murphy and Dan Levy delivered a poignant tribute to their late Home Alone and Schitt's Creek co-star and on-screen mother, Catherine O'Hara, at the Emmy Awards

Culkin remembered her as "our momma", and "like a good mom, she always showed up when I asked her to", he said.

US singer-songwriter Noah Kahan performed Bridge Over Troubled Water during the in memoriam segment on the night, before Jamie Lee Curtis paid another emotional tribute to the late actor and director Rob Reiner.

Heroes and Nashville star Hayden Panettiere, who died last month, was also remembered alongside other stars including Rocky Horror Show's Tim Curry and Dawson's Creek actor James Van Der Beek.

Emmy winner O'Hara, who died in January this year aged 71, was known for playing Culkin's frantic mother in the 1990s film franchise, as well as the eccentric Moira Rose - mum to Murphy and Levy's Alexis and David - in Schitt's Creek.

"You remember her as the forgetful mother, right?" said Culkin.

"There are all kinds of words I could use to describe Catherine. She was encouraging. She was warm. She was funny, but the word that I think of is momma... She was my mom. She was our momma."

He then reminded the audience at Los Angeles' Peacock Theater to "call your mother tonight" and urged them to "give it up for the moms", drawing cheers.

Referring to the plot of the Home Alone films, Culkin joked: "She may have forgotten me... twice! But we will always remember her."

Murphy noted how, since her death, many people had quoted O'Hara's most memorable lines from their show back at her.

"These are only very few of the interactions I've been lucky enough to have that remind me how profoundly Catherine has impacted the world, and it's because she brought us joy," Murphy said.

O'Hara's final acting role, as movie executive Patty Leigh in Seth Rogen's satire The Studio, earned her an Emmy and a Golden Globe nomination.

Levy added: "Always say yes to any opportunity to revel in the presence of greatness."

The emotional moment, which featured a giant image of a smiling O'Hara as the backdrop, appeared to bring actors Martin Short and Steve Martin, sitting in the audience, to tears.

Rob Reiner, who was killed along with his wife last year, received a posthumous Emmy last week for his guest appearance in The Bear.

A tearful Jamie Lee Curtis paid tribute to the director, writer and performer - who made films such as When Harry Met Sally, This is Spinal Tap, Stand By Me, Misery and A Few Good Men - on Monday.

She called him a "cherished legend" and "our beloved meathead", a reference to his character in the 1970s US sitcom All in the Family

The 48-year gap between Reiner's two most recent Emmy wins set a new record, beating his dad, Carl Reiner.

Curtis began her speech by first acknowledging the passing of Cheers co-creator James Burrows, who was also a good friend of Reiner's.

Elsewhere on the night, Remarkably Bright Creatures actress Sally Field led a tribute to country music star Dolly Parton, who died last month.

Field, who starred opposite Parton in the 1989 comedy drama Steel Magnolias, described her as "genuine, humble, supportive and blisteringly funny", as she introduced a special performance by country singer Reba McEntire.

"She was a humanitarian whose contribution has made a profound difference across our country," Field said of Parton, who won an Emmy herself in 2021.

"God bless you Dolly Parton my friend, I am not the only one on earth who will love you for ever and ever."

articles.title: Emmy Awards: Welsh actor Matthew Rhys makes history with double win
articles.text:
Welsh actor Matthew Rhys has made history at the Emmy Awards, becoming the first person to win two lead acting prizes in one night.

Rhys was recognised at the prestigious US ceremony for his roles in supernatural TV comedy Widow's Bay and psychological thriller The Beast In Me.

On stage, Rhys dedicated his second award "to the great and good people of Wales, who were as much a nurture as anyone else".

"We are a small but mighty nation. This is incredible," he said, adding "Diolch yn fawr iawn" - which means "thank you very much" in Welsh.

Other winners of the coveted US TV awards included Jean Smart, Allison Janney and Stephen Colbert, while there was an emotional tribute to Dolly Parton and a special humanitarian award for Michael J Fox.

Rhys was named best lead actor in a limited series for The Beast In Me, then won best lead actor in a comedy for Widow's Bay.

A small number of actors, including Alan Alda, Sally Field, John Goodman, Elisabeth Moss and Ted Danson, have previously been nominated for two lead acting prizes in the same year, but Rhys is the first to score a double win.

Backstage, he said: "I'm from a small country, and I'm glad we get moments to kind of put our flag on the map and say, 'we punch higher than our weight sometimes'."

The Beast In Me follows a grieving author, played by Claire Danes, who becomes obsessed with a mysterious new neighbour suspected of murder.

Rhys said it was a "real shock" to win the award, and told Danes: "Thank you for letting me join the mystery machine and bringing out the beast, you are an intimidating scene partner, but I'm grateful for all this."

Later in the night, accepting the comedy actor prize for playing the mayor in Widow's Bay, he thanked the family, friends and colleagues who supported his career, including his parents who "kicked me on to the stage at a very early age".

His Widow's Bay co-star Kate O'Flynn was among the other British winners, being named best supporting comedy actress for playing Patricia in the show about a fictional island beset by a centuries-old curse.

"I want to thank our mayor and all the residents of Widow's Bay, in front and behind the camera," said O'Flynn, from Bury in Greater Manchester.

She added: "This is the role of a lifetime... Thank you for trusting this Lancashire lass to play a sassy broad like Patricia."

Elsewhere, Jean Smart won best comedy actress for her role in the fifth and final series of Hacks.

It is the fifth Emmy she has won for the Hollywood satire. "What a ride this has been," Smart reflected, and joked that the audience only gave her a standing ovation "because I'm old".

It was Smart's eighth Emmy win in total, and The Diplomat's Allison Janney also picked up the eighth Emmy of her career, scoring best supporting actress in a drama series.

Smart and Janney have both now equalled the record for the most acting wins ever, shared with Cloris Leachman and Julia Louis-Dreyfus.

Despite her past success, Janney was a surprise winner on Monday and said she was "genuinely shocked" to see off competition from four stars of hospital drama The Pitt, among others.

Meanwhile, Rhea Seehorn won the first Emmy of her career for best lead actress in a drama series for Pluribus, the Apple TV show about a woman who discovers almost everyone else in the world has been taken over by a mysterious mind virus.

The Pitt won best drama, traditionally seen as the most prestigious award of the night.

And the show's leading star Noah Wyle also picked up the trophy for best lead actor in a drama series for the second year in a row.

"I'm a Hollywood kid. I was raised on a television, and movie theatres were my place of worship," Wyle told the audience. "This is all I've ever wanted to do and this is the only club I've ever wanted to join. Thank you for accepting me."

The former ER star praised all of his fellow nominees, but singled out veteran British star Sir Gary Oldman, who was nominated for Slow Horses.

Wyle said he was inspired by Sir Gary's performance as Sex Pistols bassist Sid Vicious in 1986 film Sid and Nancy, recalling how at the time he thought it was "the benchmark that I want to hit one day in my career".

Michael J Fox was given a standing ovation as he received the Bob Hope Humanitarian Award for his campaigning for support for Parkinson's disease.

The Back to the Future star, 65, who founded the Michael J Fox Foundation in 2000, said: "When it starts getting tough, you show up, you help, and if you get a little joy while you're doing it, that's even better."

Appearing in a wheelchair, he told the audience he initially kept his condition secret after being diagnosed at the age of 29.

"I worried that it would affect my work and my relationships with audiences when they laughed if they knew I was sick," he said.

But he added: "Eventually, I understood that accepting Parkinson's didn't mean I had to surrender to it. It just meant doing what I could for everyone living with this disease. So I set out to advocate for patients' needs and raise money, and to propel us towards a cure."

Macaulay Culkin, Annie Murphy and Dan Levy delivered a poignant tribute to their late Home Alone and Schitt's Creek co-star Catherine O'Hara. Culkin remembered her as "our mom", and "like a good mom, she always showed up when I asked her to".

Referring to the plot of the Home Alone films, he joked: "She may have forgotten me... twice! But we will always remember her."

Noah Kahan then performed Bridge Over Troubled Water during the in memoriam segment, before Jamie Lee Curtis paid an emotional tribute to actor and director Rob Reiner.

Reiner, who died last December, received a posthumous Emmy last week for his guest appearance in The Bear.

In other award categories, Scottish TV presenter Alan Cumming accepted the best reality show prize for the US version of The Traitors, an honour he said would encourage the team to "do better and go bigger".

"It is so beautiful that a show about treachery and betrayal brings people together," he joked, as he also thanked his dog Lala, "the perfect co-host".

On an evening otherwise light on political messages, Cumming concluded his speech by encouraging US citizens to register to vote ahead of the midterm elections in November.

Stephen Colbert won best variety series after presenting his final episode of The Late Show in May.

The presenter said nightly talk shows were a "fantastic incubator for young people to come in, work professionally, on a deadline, in collaboration, and that is the future of our business that we have to look after".

He added: "I want to say to the audience, thank you so much for watching, we hope you enjoyed the show, we had a great time doing it for you. That's it, thank you, and catch you on the flip."

articles.title: Trump says Kennedy Center to close as court rules his name must stay off building
articles.text:
The Kennedy Center board has voted to close the performing arts centre for two years, just as a US judge blocked it from adding President Donald Trump's name back to the building.

In May, the same judge ordered the removal of Trump's name and blocked its temporary closure for proposed renovations.

The board, which is chaired by Trump and includes his cabinet members and allies, approved a resolution in August to add the inscription, "Renovated and Restored by President Donald J. Trump" to the venue.

Trump announced the addition of his name to the institution, among other rebranding measures across the nation's capital, last year.

The judge's written order came less than an hour before the centre's board voted on the closure.

This was the third time it has approved closing the centre since February, amid legal challenges to Trump's work to take greater control of the institution, but there is a chance the centre's doors could stay open despite Tuesday's vote.

Trump wrote on Truth Social that the board voted "almost unanimously" to close the venue "for safety reasons".

While the closing "will take place immediately", Trump said renovations cannot begin until the court "rules on the Board's approved name" and vowed to take the case to the Supreme Court if it is a "negative" ruling.

He added that the US Department of Justice would ask for an expedited appeal and that he had raised $17m for the centre to "keep it afloat".

Also in August, the board approved a resolution to rename the campus the "President Donald J. Trump Plaza" if $100m was raised for the renovations.

Congress has approved more than $250m for renovations, as well.

However, the centre cannot close unless the federal judge, Christopher Cooper, lifts a temporary block that he put in place in May requiring it to stay open while a lawsuit brought by board member Joyce Beatty goes ahead.

Cooper had said the board could return and request the block to be lifted, provided it came to the decision to close "in a prudent manner". The request is expected to be made by Friday, CNN reported.

Beatty, an Ohio congresswoman and Democrat, said on Tuesday that the centre had planned for years to undergo phased renovations while still putting on some performances, instead of fully shutting.

She blamed Trump's attempted renaming for the departures of audiences and artists, telling the BBC he "only cares about the Kennedy Center for his vanity".

"That is wrong and it is a breach of his fiduciary duty as a trustee. Congress established the Kennedy Center as a living memorial to President Kennedy, and I am proud to defend this cherished institution."

In February 2025, Trump replaced several trustees on the board, which then decided in December to rename the institution. New lettering bearing Trump's full name was affixed to the centre's front portico the following day.

The changes were followed by cancellations by artists booked at the venue and a drop in ticket sales.

articles.title: Ed Sheeran wants to stay out of politics. By quitting his tour, his support acts have exposed the hollowness of neutrality
articles.text:
In a statement about Macklemore being dropped from his US stadium tour for making pro-Palestinian comments, Ed Sheeran defended his own publicly apolitical stance: “If we only ever focus on shouting the loudest, nothing will ever change. There are different approaches to being an advocate for change.”

Every other musician involved with the tour – support acts Finneas (Billie Eilish’s brother), Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish songwriter Aaron Rowe, plus Sheeran’s Irish backing band, Beoga – has made their approach to advocating for change clear, pulling out of the remaining dates to protest against the censorship of Macklemore and to express support for the Palestinian people.

In a statement released yesterday, Sheeran stressed that it wasn’t his decision to remove Macklemore, who called for a free Palestine on stage at the MetLife stadium in New Jersey last week. “I am not complicit,” Sheeran wrote. Macklemore (who in 2014 had to apologise after being accused of perpetuating antisemitic stereotypes with an onstage costume) wrote that his removal from the tour was organised by New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft, who owns Gillette Stadium outside Boston, where Sheeran’s Loop tour is due to play in late September.

Kraft confirmed he barred Macklemore from opening for Sheeran at the Gillette Stadium, but did not respond to claims he organised the boycott by the other venues. (In a statement he said his decision was “not about diminishing the suffering of innocent Palestinians or denying anyone the right to advocate on their behalf” but that such advocacy “should not obscure the responsibility of Hamas”.)

Sheeran explained that he doesn’t use his platform for politics in order to be “a place of safety and sanctuary, to maintain diplomacy and keep conversations open”. Though this isn’t accurate: he performed at the Concert for Ukraine in 2022, signed an open letter to Theresa May about Brexit, endorsed Jeremy Corbyn and supported the equality act in the US.

Either way, the consequences of his apolitical stance have proven beyond doubt that there is no such thing as a neutral position, especially when you’re operating in a political culture that rarely obstructs corporate overreach. Kraft is friends with Trump and is a major donor to Israel: Netanyahu said at a 2019 awards ceremony honouring Kraft that “Israel does not have a more loyal friend”.

The decisive actions of every other musician on the tour have made a mockery of Sheeran claiming to be powerless in this situation. In his statement, Sheeran wrote that he would never “let down the fans who had made plans” by cancelling shows, “nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living”. What might initially appear as a sign of solidarity – not inconveniencing fans, not leaving other artists and crew out of pocket – has been upended by a group of artists who understand that losing financial and professional opportunities and creating inconvenience is precisely what it takes to show backbone and stand against genocide and billionaires crushing free speech.

Macklemore’s speech in New Jersey introduced his 2024 song Hind’s Hall, which castigates censorship of protest against Israel’s genocide in Palestine, particularly the student encampment at Columbia University in New York, and is named after Hind Rajab, a five-year-old Palestinian girl killed by Israeli forces. “What you willin’ to risk?” he asked in the song. “What you willin’ to give?” Many musicians and actors who have spoken out against Israel’s actions in Gaza have talked about losing work as a result: Susan Sarandon said last week at the Venice film festival that she has had acting gigs taken away; Irish pop star CMAT said a lucrative beauty contract was withdrawn; Swedish star Zara Larsson said she was dropped from brand deals and awards shows.

That hasn’t stopped them and other figures from continuing to speak out, putting moral imperative above personal gain, and recognising that any such “loss” bears no relation to what is happening to human life and habitat in Gaza, where Israel’s military offensive is estimated to have led to a death toll of 70,000. Dublin songwriter Aaron Rowe, by far the smallest support act on Sheeran’s tour and thus the one with the most to lose, thanked him for the life-changing opportunity. “But as Irish people we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation,” his statement continued. “I need to be true to myself and my ancestors who resisted colonisation, and fought for a freedom that I enjoy today in Ireland.”

Sheeran and countless others take the line that pop culture should be somewhere fans can go to escape politics. “I do understand that for a lot of people, they just want to leave politics aside for a bit and be able to enjoy the music,” culture secretary Lisa Nandy said of the Sheeran situation on LBC this morning. But the fact that most right-wing politicians also take that view indicates the fact that they see pop cultural figures, with their largely left-leaning views and huge reach among young people, as a genuine threat best silenced.

As Democratic congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said yesterday, this isn’t just about the musicians on Sheeran’s tour, but “how just a handful of stadium owners can prevent [discussion of] an entire massive issue, in this case, the genocide in Gaza”. Prominent figures who go along with that view and deny the power of their voice allow these billion-dollar corporations to rob us of our rights step by step until one day there is nothing left. “We need to be very clear about how dangerous a precedent this is,” said Ocasio-Cortez.

At worst, Sheeran – who has always been open about his commercially minded approach to pop – looks like a corporate shill; at best, wilfully naive. Sheeran loves to dabble in the music of other cultures to present a toothless pan-global vision of togetherness lifted from the latter-day Coldplay playbook. But you can’t play with the aesthetics of global music without also being willing to engage in the lived reality of those cultures.

“Those who have been to one of my shows will know that they are about unity, joy, escapism, love and a place for everyone to feel welcome,” Sheeran wrote in his statement. Just as long as they shut up and sing: Sheeran’s inaction and humiliation at the hands of his principled supporting musicians have irrevocably compromised a position that’s no longer fit for purpose, if it ever was.

articles.title: Your mission, Tom Cruise, is to improve at interviews. And please keep sending the cakes
articles.text:
By now, we’ve grown used to watching Tom Cruise excel at everything he does. Running in films? The best. Risking his life in action scenes so preposterously dangerous that audiences need to have their sphincters manually unclenched with a crowbar? Absolutely, none better. Singlehandedly ensuring that theatrical exhibition didn’t go extinct after Covid? The man deserves all the praise in the world for that.

But nobody is perfect. Live long enough and a few flaws will worm their way to the surface. This is as true for Tom Cruise as it is for anyone else. And while I realise that this might do me out of a cake this Christmas, the following really needs to be said: Tom Cruise isn’t very good at interviews.

As you will be aware, Cruise’s new film Digger comes out soon. The film is a risk. It is his first original, non-sequel, non-action film in which he co-stars since 2007’s Lions for Lambs. It is also, if the trailers are any indication, palpably batshit. This means that Cruise has to reintroduce himself to the world as an actor, rather than the guy who just flings himself off a variety of increasingly berserk surfaces. And this means promotion. Until this week, that promotion has involved either World Cup-themed promos filmed in character or interviews where the subject matter was almost exclusively limited to lens choice.

However, yesterday Cruise subjected himself to a rare longform interview opposite GQ’s Zach Baron. On paper, it couldn’t have been easier. Baron was a perfectly chosen interviewer for the job, understanding exactly when to flatter and when to needle. However, Tom Cruise’s defences are foot-thick and watertight, and the majority of Baron’s questions simply bounced off him.

This resulted in a fairly unsatisfactory 30-minute stalemate in which Tom Cruise talked and talked and said nothing at all. No matter how hard Baron probed, he was met with a fat wedge of waffle. The clickbait industrial complex has done its best to pick the bones of the interview for a news peg, but the best it seems to have come up with is a variation of “Tom Cruise admits that he can be intense on set”. Which, well, duh.

Aside from that, we simply got a rehash of all the old talking points from every junket he’s done for a decade. He’d rather talk about cinematography than himself. He is constantly trying to learn new skills. He writes down his dreams and how to accomplish them. None of this is new information. It’s all highly frustrating. But it does make sense. As brilliant as he is on screen, behind the scenes Cruise is a carefully managed enigma. This may well be because, the last time he allowed his own self to parade before the press, it ended with couch-jumping and excruciatingly testy interviews about Scientology. It seems unthinkable now, but that press run went so badly that Sumner Redstone ended up effectively firing Cruise from Paramount over it.

It took Cruise years to build himself back up from that, and the results have been spectacular. The Mission: Impossible films have been some of the greatest of his career. Top Gun: Maverick saved Hollywood. He is now in a position of enormous power and authority. So going back out in front of an interviewer is bound to be a risk for him. But one thing is certain. The Digger promotional cycle cannot just be variations of the GQ interview, because too many opaque soundbites will simply end up boring potential audiences rigid. There will be more interviews – he’s thought to be hitting the podcast circuit soon – so he needs to adapt his strategy.

The good news is that one thing Cruise did say in his GQ interview is that, when he sets a goal, he writes down all the steps necessary to accomplish it. This is exactly what he should do here. If his dream is doing press that will make people want to watch Digger, then he knows he will need to work up some new anecdotes – long enough to filibuster, but twisty enough to entertain – while developing a persona that appears to welcome scrutiny while wriggling out from underneath it.

It can be done. Robert Downey Jr is an actor with many areas of his past he would rather not touch in print, and he has built up an incredibly charming suit of armour that allows him to breezily bat questions away when they get too personal. This is exactly what Tom Cruise should be learning to do. Or perhaps not; after all, he has made hundreds of millions of dollars by revealing scarcely anything about himself for a decade. Maybe that’s an option, too.

But, hey, this is Tom Cruise. When he sets his mind on something, he achieves it. With that in mind, expect a dramatic upward turn in the quality of his interviews from this moment onwards. Thanks for reading. Please still send cakes.
